clips.title: JWT Explained In Under 10 Minutes (JSON Web Tokens)
clips.why: A clear explanation of what a JWT is made of, which is exactly what the App signs in the lab.
look: The three parts: header, payload and signature, joined by dots.
How the signature proves that nobody changed the token after it was signed.
That a JWT is encoded, not encrypted: anyone can read the payload.
clips.after: The broker signs a JWT like this with the App's private key, and GitHub checks it with the public half before handing out a one-hour token.

clips.title: Introduction to GitHub Actions - Part 6 - Repository Rulesets
clips.why: Mickey Gousset creates a repository ruleset step by step, with a required check and a pull request rule.
look: The three parts of a ruleset: which branches, which rules, and who may bypass.
How a required status check is chosen by its name.
How the ruleset is aimed at the default branch.
clips.after: fcp's main ruleset is the same form, written as JSON and applied once by an org admin, with no bypass for the agents' App.

clips.title: GitHub branch rules (protect your git branches)
clips.why: A short tour of the two rules that matter most for us: a pull request before merging, and checks that must pass.
look: Requiring a pull request, with approvals, before anything is merged.
Choosing the checks that must pass before a merge.
This is the older branch protection screen; rulesets offer the same rules and more.
clips.after: Our ruleset uses these rules plus 'the last pusher cannot approve', so nothing new can land after a review.

practice.q: Put the steps of one agent push to GitHub in order.
items: The broker reads the App's private key from Vault when it starts
A run asks the broker to push nova/RH-1234
The broker signs a JWT that says it is the App, valid for a few minutes
GitHub checks the signature and returns an installation token for fcp only, valid for one hour
The broker pushes with that token; the VM never sees it
practice.why: The key never leaves the broker. The JWT only proves who the App is; the installation token is what acts, and it is narrowed and short.

practice.q: Finish the mint call so the token works on one repo only.
practice.hint: The option of @octokit/auth-app that lists repos by name.
practice.why: repositoryNames narrows the installation token to those repos, even if the App is installed on more.

practice.q: The App's permission list has no workflows entry. Nova's run changes .github/workflows/frontend-ci.yaml and pushes. What happens?

options.text: The push works, because contents: write covers every file
options.why: Workflow files are special. Changing them needs the workflows permission, which the App does not have.
Without the workflows permission, GitHub rejects any push from the App that touches .github/workflows, so an agent cannot rewrite the CI that judges it.

options.text: The push works, but the workflow does not run
options.why: GitHub refuses the whole push. Nothing about the workflow changes.

practice.q: A teammate proposes adding the App to the bypass list, 'so Nova can merge its own PRs when everything is green'. What do you answer?

options.text: Fine, green checks are proof enough
options.why: Checks prove the tests pass, not that a person agreed with the change. The rule is one approval from someone independent.

options.text: Only in bypass_mode pull_request, so it is logged
options.why: A logged bypass is still a bypass. Agents never merge; the only bypass is the two-person break-glass team.

options.text: No: agents never merge, and a bypass would skip the one human approval
options.why: The whole design rests on a person approving and merging. A bypass for the App would remove that wall for every run.

practice.q: Finish the rule that cancels an approval when a new commit is pushed.
practice.hint: Four words joined by underscores: dismiss, stale, reviews, on push.
practice.why: Without it, an approval given to an earlier commit would still count after new code arrives.

practice.q: Three workflows each have a job named Unit Tests. Which name should the ruleset require?

options.text: Unit Tests, once, because it covers all three
options.why: A required check is one name. GitHub cannot tell which of the three jobs it means.

options.text: Distinct names, after renaming the jobs to Cloud, Client and Frontend Unit Tests
options.why: Each required check must match exactly one job's name, so the jobs get unique names first.

options.text: The workflow file names instead of the job names
options.why: Required checks match the check name the PR shows, which comes from the job's name, not the file name.
